I'm Mohit, and I want to explain the part people never understand: why I kept paying.
The first transfer was small, ₹2,000, for a trading course a friendly man recommended in a group chat. The next week my account showed profits. To withdraw them, there was a fee. Then a "wallet upgrade". Then a "clearance charge". Each payment was bigger than the last.
By then I'd put in more than ₹90,000. Every time I thought of stopping, I felt sick: stopping meant saying out loud that I, the one my family called sensible, had been fooled. Paying one more time felt less painful than admitting it.
That's what they count on. Not greed. Pride.
It only stopped when I asked my old friend Pankaj to lend me money for the "final fee", and Pankaj said, "I'll give you nothing for that. But I'll sit with you while you call the bank."

Mahima

Thanks for having me on the college radio, Alka. People ask why I talk about being scammed so openly. Honestly, a year ago I couldn't. I'd lost ₹40,000 to a fake customs officer who said my parcel held contraband. I felt like an idiot. I was angry for months, mostly at myself.
What changed was my family. My father, who I was sure would shout, said, "You were targeted by professionals. That's a crime, not a character flaw." My cousin told me the same thing had happened to her boss, a chartered accountant. That's when I understood it wasn't about being stupid. These people are trained to work on fear.
So now I say it plainly: urgency, secrecy, threats, payment. If you hear those four together, hang up and call someone you trust.
I'm Devika, and if my story saves one person listening tonight, that money bought something after all.

qa.a: You were targeted by professionals. That's a crime, not a character flaw.

qa.q: What pattern does Devika teach listeners to spot?
qa.a: Urgency, secrecy, threats and payment together; when all four appear, hang up and call someone trusted.

qa.a: Alka likely feels proud and grateful, seeing Devika turn a painful loss into a warning for others.

grounding: Family who call a scam a crime, not a flaw, help a young adult recover from shame and anger and share the story publicly.

"We've got enough," Thomas said, and ran to the pitch.
The PE teacher was busy with the other class. Varun sat on the steps near the water cooler. From there he could hear the bat hitting the ball and everyone shouting. Last year he and Thomas had been bowling partners.

When the bell rang, a classmate asked why he hadn't played. "Didn't feel like it," Varun said, looking away.

Noor sent Mehak a long message at 7 p.m. about the science project. By 9 there was no reply, though the ticks showed it had been read. Noor lay on her bed in their Delhi flat and replayed the day. Mehak had laughed at lunch when Noor spilled her juice. Not a mean laugh, maybe. But maybe.
By 10 Noor had decided: Mehak was tired of her. Everyone probably was.
Next morning in class Mehak waved. "Sorry, my phone died after I read it, and then Mummy made me do the dishes." Noor heard only the sorry and nodded stiffly. "It's fine. I'll do the project myself."
Mehak's smile faded. "Oh. Okay."
Noor went back to her desk, stomach tight. See, she thought. She doesn't even care. She didn't notice that it was her own cold voice that had closed the door.

qa.a: Her phone died after she read it, and then Mummy made her do the dishes.

qa.a: Noor felt lonely and rejected, reading the late reply and the lunch laugh as proof Mehak was tired of her.

qa.a: Remind herself of other reasons, like a dead phone, and ask Mehak warmly instead of pulling away.

qa.a: Mehak likely feels confused and hurt, pushed away after a genuine apology.

grounding: A lonely teen reads a late reply and a laugh as dislike, turns guarded, and her coldness makes the rejection she feared more likely.
